concepts.name: BIS Origins, Ownership Structure, and Legal Status
key_dimensions: Founded in 1930 under the Hague Agreements — oldest international financial institution (not IMF/World Bank trap)
Ownership: shares held by central banks, NOT governments — majority owned by member central banks (~60 central banks)
Legal status: international organization with sovereign immunity, headquartered in Basel, Switzerland (not an EU body)
Original mandate (reparation payments under Young Plan) vs. evolved mandate — UPSC trap on historical purpose

concepts.name: BIS Core Mandate and Functions
key_dimensions: Primary mandate: fostering monetary and financial stability — NOT development finance (contrast with World Bank)
Three core functions: banker to central banks, forum for central bank cooperation, research/statistics hub
Does NOT lend to governments or commercial banks — only to central banks and international organizations
Distinction from IMF: BIS does not provide balance-of-payments support or have surveillance conditionality

concepts.name: BIS as 'Bank for Central Banks' — Banking Services
key_dimensions: Holds foreign exchange and gold reserves on behalf of member central banks
Provides short-term credit facilities to central banks facing liquidity stress
Manages reserve portfolios and offers investment services exclusively to central banks
UPSC trap: BIS does NOT accept deposits from or lend to private banks or the public

concepts.name: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) — Relationship with BIS
key_dimensions: BCBS is hosted by BIS but is a separate body — members are banking supervisors, not BIS per se
BCBS sets global standards for bank regulation (Basel Accords) — BIS provides secretariat support
Membership distinction: BCBS has ~45 members; BIS has ~60 central bank members — overlap but not identical
UPSC trap: Basel norms are BCBS outputs, not BIS outputs directly — attribution error common

concepts.name: Basel I, II, and III Accords — Evolution of Capital Adequacy Framework
key_dimensions: Basel I (1988): focused solely on credit risk; introduced 8% minimum Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR)
Basel II (2004): three-pillar structure — minimum capital requirements, supervisory review, market discipline; added operational and market risk
Basel III (2010, post-GFC): introduced Capital Conservation Buffer, Countercyclical Buffer, Leverage Ratio, LCR, NSFR
UPSC trap: Basel III was a response to 2008 GFC inadequacies of Basel II — sequence and rationale critical

concepts.name: Basel III Capital Buffers and Liquidity Standards
key_dimensions: Capital Conservation Buffer: 2.5% of RWAs — must be maintained above minimum CAR; breach restricts dividends
Countercyclical Capital Buffer (CCyB): 0–2.5% — activated by national regulators during credit booms
Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR): ensures sufficient High-Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA) for 30-day stress scenario
Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR): long-term liquidity metric — available stable funding ≥ required stable funding over 1 year

concepts.name: Systemically Important Banks (G-SIBs) and Additional Surcharges under Basel III
key_dimensions: G-SIBs (Global Systemically Important Banks) identified annually by FSB using BCBS methodology
Additional Loss Absorbency surcharge: 1%–3.5% additional CET1 capital over and above Basel III minimums
Five categories/buckets of G-SIBs based on systemic importance score — bucket 5 currently empty (deterrence design)
UPSC trap: D-SIBs (Domestic SIBs) are identified by national regulators (RBI in India), not BCBS/BIS directly

concepts.name: Total Loss-Absorbing Capacity (TLAC) and MREL — Post-Crisis Resolution Frameworks
key_dimensions: TLAC standard (FSB, endorsed by G20 2015): G-SIBs must hold minimum 16%→18% of RWAs in bail-in-able instruments
Purpose: ensure private-sector loss absorption during resolution without taxpayer bailouts
MREL (Minimum Requirement for own funds and Eligible Liabilities) — EU equivalent of TLAC under BRRD
UPSC trap: TLAC is an FSB standard (not BCBS/BIS directly) but closely linked — institutional attribution matters

concepts.name: BIS Governance: Board of Directors and General Manager
key_dimensions: Board of Directors: composed of governors of major central banks (ex-officio members + elected members)
Ex-officio members include governors of central banks of Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, UK, USA — founding members
General Manager heads BIS management — appointed by Board, not elected by member central banks
Annual General Meeting (AGM): held in Basel, attended by member central bank representatives — key decision-making forum

concepts.name: BIS Committees and Research Bodies — The BIS 'Family'
key_dimensions: Key committees hosted: BCBS, CPMI (payments), CGFS (financial stability), Markets Committee, Irving Fisher Committee
Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures (CPMI): standards for payment, clearing, settlement systems
Committee on the Global Financial System (CGFS): monitors global financial markets — provides data to policymakers
UPSC trap: FSB (Financial Stability Board) is NOT a BIS committee — it is a separate G20-created body, also based in Basel

concepts.name: Financial Stability Board (FSB) — Relationship with BIS and G20
key_dimensions: FSB established in 2009 (G20 London Summit) — successor to Financial Stability Forum (FSF, 1999)
FSB Secretariat is housed at BIS premises in Basel — but FSB is legally/institutionally separate from BIS
FSB mandate: monitor and make recommendations about global financial system — coordinates with IMF, BCBS, IOSCO
UPSC trap: FSF was created after 1997 Asian crisis; FSB after 2008 GFC — both housed at BIS but distinct bodies

concepts.name: BIS Innovation Hub (BISIH) — Digital Finance Initiatives
key_dimensions: Established in 2019 — works on central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), DeFi regulation, green finance tech
Network of centres in Singapore, Hong Kong, London, Stockholm, Toronto, Eurosystem, NY Fed, etc.
Project mBridge: multi-CBDC platform (BIS + Hong Kong, Thailand, UAE, China central banks) for cross-border payments
UPSC relevance: BIS Innovation Hub signals BIS evolution beyond traditional roles into fintech policy architecture

concepts.name: BIS Quarterly Review and Annual Economic Report — Research and Statistical Role
key_dimensions: BIS Quarterly Review: key source of global banking statistics, derivatives data, international debt securities data
BIS Annual Economic Report: flagship publication — analyzes global monetary conditions, financial stability risks
BIS maintains the most comprehensive database on OTC derivatives, cross-border banking, and global liquidity
UPSC angle: BIS research outputs (e.g., on crypto risks, climate financial risks) often form basis of Prelims data questions

concepts.name: Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures (PFMIs) — CPMI-IOSCO Standards
key_dimensions: PFMIs (2012): jointly issued by CPMI (BIS) and IOSCO — global standards for systemically important FMIs
Covers: Central Counterparties (CCPs), Central Securities Depositories (CSDs), payment systems, trade repositories
24 principles covering legal basis, governance, credit risk, liquidity risk, settlement finality, etc.
UPSC trap: PFMIs are NOT Basel norms — separate framework for market infrastructure vs. bank capital regulation

concepts.name: India's Engagement with BIS and Basel Norms Implementation
key_dimensions: Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is a member of BIS and participates in BCBS — India part of BCBS since 2009
India's Basel III implementation: RBI adopted Basel III framework with phased implementation (2013 onwards, fully by 2019)
Indian banks' CAR requirements: minimum 9% (higher than Basel III's 8%) — RBI's conservative approach
UPSC trap: India follows Basel norms through RBI regulation, NOT directly from BIS/BCBS — implementation is domestic

concepts.name: BIS and Gold — Historical and Contemporary Role
key_dimensions: BIS is one of the largest official holders of gold in the world — holds gold on behalf of member central banks
Historical role: facilitated gold settlements during Bretton Woods system and pre-war reparations era
BIS gold accounts allow central banks to conduct gold swaps, deposits, and sight accounts
UPSC angle: BIS role in gold distinguishes it from IMF (which holds gold as reserve asset in SDR basket context)

concepts.name: Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) vs. BIS Reserve Management — Institutional Distinction
key_dimensions: SDRs are IMF instruments — BIS does NOT issue SDRs; this is a common UPSC trap
BIS manages reserves in conventional currencies (USD, EUR, GBP, JPY) and gold — no SDR management role
BIS can act as fiscal agent for international financial arrangements but IMF handles quota/SDR allocations
Distinction: IMF = macroeconomic surveillance + BoP support; BIS = microprudential standards + central bank banking

concepts.name: Countercyclical Macroprudential Policy — BIS Conceptual Contributions
key_dimensions: BIS economists (Claudio Borio et al.) pioneered the concept of 'financial cycle' distinct from business cycle
BIS research underpins macroprudential tools: CCyB, Loan-to-Value (LTV) caps, Debt-Service Ratios
BIS Annual Reports regularly warn about 'too-loose-for-too-long' monetary policy and asset price bubbles
UPSC angle: BIS positions itself as advocate for early tightening — contrasts with IMF's more growth-accommodative stance

concepts.name: Crypto-Assets and Stablecoins — BIS Regulatory Position
key_dimensions: BIS has consistently flagged crypto-assets as financial stability risks — published multiple critical working papers
Prudential treatment of banks' crypto exposures: BCBS standard (2022) — Group 1 (tokenized traditional assets) vs. Group 2 (unbacked crypto) with 1250% risk weight for Group 2
BIS supports CBDCs as public alternative to private stablecoins — 'singleness of money' principle
UPSC trap: The 1250% risk weight for unbacked crypto is a BCBS standard, not a domestic RBI rule — though RBI may adopt

concepts.name: Climate-Related Financial Risks and BIS — Green Swan Concept
key_dimensions: BIS introduced the 'Green Swan' concept (2020 report) — climate risks as extreme, unpredictable systemic financial risks (vs. Black Swan)
Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS): separate body but BIS supports its work on climate stress testing
BIS research: physical risks (extreme weather) and transition risks (policy shifts) both pose systemic bank risks
UPSC angle: Green Swan vs. Black Swan distinction — BIS's framing that climate risks are categorically different from typical tail risks
